newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - US Sept durables orders up 4.6 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - US Sept durables orders up 4.6 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department repeorted orders for durable goods in September rose 4.6 percent, the largest increase since December of 1992.
U.S. economists in a Reuters survey had expected orders to rise 2.0 percent.

WILLIAM SHULTZ, W.R. LAZARD AND CO: "Certainly it's tough to poke holes (in this report). It looks strong throughout ... It's going to keep the (Federal Reserve) nervous going into the next (policy-setting) meeting" on November 13.

DAVID SLOAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, I.D.E.A. INC: "It seems 60 percent of the gain was in aircraft. The ex-transport figure up 0.9 percent after a 1.8 percent fall is not that impressive ... There does seem to be some gain in autos. It's a stronger-than-expected figure, but when you look at the breakdown it's nothing remarkable ... mainly due to aircraft."
DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "No matter how you cut this number, you still have the manufacturing sector recovering from last month's blow."

Seto continued: "One example of that, excluding aircraft, you've got a 3.1-percent increase recovering from last month's 4.9-percent decline. So the underlying trend, for most of the manufacturers, is still upwards ... this month, we are getting a significant boost from the aircraft sector."

WALDO BEST, SENIOR ECNOMIST, BZW SECURITIES INC: "The only surprise is in civilian aircraft which is high as a result of Boeing's recent string of orders being lumped into one month. The overall number suggests goods production is still moderate and does not demand any immediate attention from the Fed."
KEVIN FLANAGAN, FIRST VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "No doubt the numbers are stronger than expected.

"The (Treasury) market will have some problems with the figure ... not quite sure it creates any significant selling pressure at this time, especially considering the number of challenges ahead next week, but one can see this morning's report keeping a lid on where the Treasury market's going to go today and actually exert some downward pressure on prices overall.

Flanagan continued: "We found out that businesses still remain upbeat with respect to the economy and that's coming through in their actions by boosting orders ... and it wasn't just transportation and aircraft either; we did have some gains in other sectors like electrical machinery.
"Looking ahead, something like the backlog in shipments suggests that the economy is probably not as weak as the market's pricing mechanism is assuming," he added.
